title: Payroll run
brief: On pay day your system tells the payment rail to move salaries for two million employees, then publishes a payslip for each one. Employees open the app at breakfast to see if they were paid. Paying anyone twice is the one thing you must never do.

clarify.q: How fast does the payment rail accept transfers?
clarify.a: About 1,000 per second on your account, and sometimes it asks you to slow down to half for a while.

clarify.q: Does a salary have to arrive the second we send it?
clarify.a: No. Money may settle later that day. What matters is that each salary is paid exactly once.
Very. Salaries and bank details must be encrypted with keys held in a key service.

notes: Payments go to a payment rail provider with its own limit.

numbers.label: Rail limit while it is slowing you down
Payments waiting after one hour of the slowdown

hints: The rail can take 1,000 payments a second, and sometimes only 500. What can hold the extra payments safely until the rail is ready?
A queue between your servers and a worker pool lets the workers send at the pace the rail allows. Only the rail call needs the queue; pages and logins can stay direct.
Servers send payments to a queue; workers check an idempotency store, then call the rail, so a retried message never pays twice. Keep payslip files in object storage and add a key service.

editorial.summary: Everything is easy except the payment rail. It accepts about 1,000 transfers a second and may halve that without warning. The fix is a queue: the servers say "accepted", the workers pay at the rail's pace, and an idempotency key on each payment makes a retried message harmless. Payslips are files, so they go to object storage.

designs.name: Queue the payments, key every one
designs.why: Servers answer employees quickly. Payments and payslips become messages. Workers check the idempotency store, then call the rail or write the payslip file, and the queue holds the backlog while the rail is slow.

tradeoffs: The queue turns a payment into "accepted, will be paid today". Employees see the status change later, which is fine for salaries and wrong for a card checkout.
Workers are sized for the average payment rate, not the burst. A bigger pool would only make the rail refuse more calls.
Idempotency keys cost a lookup per payment and remove the double-pay bug, which is the failure that makes headlines.
Payslip files are cheap in object storage, about 2 cents per GB per month, so keeping every payslip for years costs very little.
editorial.realWorld: Payroll providers move billions of dollars on a single pay-day morning and still treat "paid twice" as an incident, so every payment carries a unique key (approx.).
